To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the norms and practices in each country are different and, within each country, the practices of different cities vary significantly.

(1) there is diversity between the norms of the three countries and IPSAS; (2) there is diversity in the practices between cities; and (3) there is diversity within cities, with the practices of different departments within a single city varying considerably.

there was a lack of comparability of the accrual policies for infrastructure, art, and heritage assets in the financial statements of six cities across three countries, and a lack of comparably between the practices of the six cities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how far the diversity of practice in financial reporting of local governments in Europe is driven by national norms, and the extent to which it is driven by other factors.
the question of whether there is a need to develop a new standard for local government accounting in Europe.
how the financial statements for infrastructure, art, and heritage assets are prepared and presented in six European cities, and how this relates to national norms and international best practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the normative and practical diversity is so wide and so varied that it is impossible to make any generalisations about it.

the diversity of practice in the reporting of infrastructure, art and cultural heritage assets is such that there can be no general statement about the comparability of financial reporting between cities or between countries.
there is no clear evidence that accrual accounting norms have had an impact on the financial statements of local governments in our three countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diversity of accrual accounting policies in local government is greater than we expected.
there is a significant divergence of practice in the reporting of infrastructure, art and cultural assets in the three countries, with a number of cities reporting in a non‐compliant manner.

the diversity of practices is such that it is difficult to see how any of the norms or practices could be described as best practice, although it is clear that the practices of many of the cities are not consistent with the norms of either their own governments or of IPSAS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diversity of norms and practices is so great that the notion of a single ‘best practice’ is not helpful.
there is a need to understand the reasons behind the diversity we observed, to determine whether the diversity is justified or not.
the norms and practices in this area are diverse, and that the diversity is not explained by the norms of national accounting standards.
